utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: First of all, before we proceed to the taking of evidence today, you will all observe that Judge Moloto, our Presiding Judge, is not with us. He is elsewhere on business touching and concerning the Tribunal, and under those circumstances, Judge Hoepfel and I have elected to proceed under Rule 15 bis, and that is the position today. We are anticipating that Judge Moloto will join us by the third session today. If not, certainly tomorrow. And Mr. McElligott, you are in the thick of your evidence, being cross-examined. You are reminded that your declaration is still operating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you were in the thick of your cross-examination. You indicated yesterday you were somewhere towards the end and that you anticipated completion by the end of the first session. Did I understand you correctly yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are very close to the end, and I believe that we will finish by mid-second session. I'll try to be as efficient as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're reminded of the guidelines, of course, and to try and keep within them. That is the caution that the Chamber is issuing to you. Please do proceed now. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McElligott. We shall proceed with your cross-examination. Yesterday we left it off with the special police. During your examination-in-chief, you were shown document Exhibit 730 and you recognised it as the organigramme of the police in sector 7. Can we please see the document on the screen? Before we see the document on the screen, I shall remind you that based on the document representing the organigramme of the police in Sector North, you said that there was regular police that was in charge of keeping law and order and other policing work. According to the document, there were 7.000 police officers in that group, and there was also special police that were in charge of the protection of borders and prevention of terrorism. According to the document, there were 16.000 special policemen. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Milovancevic. We are not getting the document on our screens. Please go on in the interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now we can see the document on the screen, Your Honour. Can we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. McElligott? This is the document that I was referring to. It is here that the regular police is mentioned as well as the units of the special police. In this regard, I would like to ask you which of the two groups was dealing with the customary police work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the group -- there was -- please raise the chart. Just a moment. What I call the regular police are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the bottom of the page, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just raise it a little, yeah. You have the special police and you have the border police. What we had is one group which is projected there as a group of about 7.000. I regarded that within that group, there were policemen who were dressed in what I would call normal police uniforms. That within them there was certainly a number of them who were seen by our police officers to be professional police officers who were -- had experience in policing. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. This will do. The regular police, was it under the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina, the 7.000 police officers that you are referring to at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We regarded the entire group to be within the authority of the Knin authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We shall come back to the entire group a little later. Now I would like to know whether you know that this regular police was on the strength of the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina. I'm talking about the regular police only. Were they under the MUP of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, going back to the -- what we saw was a full component of Milicija, and one group, as I say, was regarded as -- within them was a group of police officers who had policing experience, and there was another group that we regarded as a totally different group in a sense that we felt they never had policing experience in any way. They seemed to have a different agenda, a different approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: On what do you base this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the dealings that our police monitors had with them on a one-to-one, on the ground, when they were doing their patrols, the way they were treated, and it was the general view that was established from all those activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: For example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have had monitors who were stopped at check-points and abused. I can recall one incident where our police monitors were stopped and held at gun-point, and he was -- actually, the interpreter, a female, who got in between them and our monitors and negotiated a solution to it. I know that those monitors were extremely frightened and stressed by the consequences of the approach that was taken to them. We have had incidents where they would just slow down, were obstructed, weren't allowed their freedom of movement as they were entitled to. I can recall one incident where monitors were not permitted through a check-point and the reasons given were that they had not actually supplied the serial number of their radio, of their car radio, the communications radio. So that type of approach was taken by a particular group. They were what we regarded as the special police. Within the other group, there were people that we regarded as having policing experience. There was a degree of professionalism about them and indeed there was a good degree of contact. They were -- let's put it this way. There was a helpful approach coming. And they were -- you know, in some places they were there for quite a while. On occasions we had relationships built up and then the people would move and you were back to square one again. So you had two different groups there and you had two different approaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic, would you like to pick up again or anything arising out of what the witness has answered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that you agree that one can say that the regular police belonged to the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK. Is there any doubt about that or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is that both sides belonged to the RSK, that they were in the control of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior of the RSK was Mr. Martic; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You already said, and you have repeated today, that the regular police consisted of the professional police officers who performed those duties even before the break-up of the former Yugoslavia and that the UNCIVPOL had very good cooperation with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes. Cooperation with some of those people, yes. And within that group, we recognised that there were people who had a professional policing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. The second group that you referred to as units of the special police, according to the chart before you, did they deal with the tasks that do not customarily fall within the purview of the police work but rather within the purview of the military? Would you agree with that? Can you scroll down a little so that Mr. McElligott has the full picture? Can I see the bottom of the page, the whole remark at the bottom of the document, the note?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group, Your Honour, were functioning within the United Nations protection area and we regarded them as Milicija. They were -- we -- the whole group was regarded as the police component, but there was a divide. And the divide was one of how they functioned, how they performed with the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer the part of the question which was according to your knowledge, were these people involved in the policing or in some other tasks? We are talking about the protection of the borders and the protection of the population against terrorist attacks. What was that? Was that policing or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were carrying out check-points within the United Nations protection area and in reality we regarded that as part of the policing function. It would be checking movement of people and patrolling the areas and we regarded that as a policing function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You emphasised, you highlighted, members of this group as the cause of all the problems that occurred in the area. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All the problems in the area? I'm sorry, your opponent is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't recall this being the verbatim testimony and I would appreciate a cite to make sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. For precision, Mr. Milovancevic, could we get the citation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't been precise. I meant paragraph 29 of the witness's statement. Can the usher please provide the witness with a copy of the statement he gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I'm referring to paragraph 29 of your statement, where, in the middle, you say: "Reports from CIVPOL monitors show that the special police in active in creating the unacceptable conditions that Martic refers to and that they continued to pursue these activities." My question to you, sir, was relative to that part of your statement. I apologise for not being precise in my previous question. And my question with regard to that part of your statement is as follows: You highlighted members of the special police as the cause of those problems in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. You joined the UNPROFOR mission in October 1992 and you left in November 1993. During that time, did the special police units existed [as interpreted]? Throughout the period, that is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm aware of is that there were people or people in uniform carrying a variety of arms that were in contravention of the Vance Plan and that they were functioning throughout the protected areas, and these are the people that we regarded as special police, and these are the ones our monitors regarded as special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is what you believed. However, are you aware of the fact that special units of the police in October -- in November 1992, the latest, became part of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? I'm talking about Exhibit 576 that has been admitted into evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm accounting for are the people that our monitors met on the ground. Indeed I saw them myself when I was in visiting stations and they were regarded as special police. They were regarded as the Milicija, and people saw them as a group different to what they were regarded the professional police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And did you see them throughout the whole of the time that was put to you by counsel, October 1992 and November 1993? You have not effectively addressed that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. At this stage I'm not sure when I saw them or when I didn't see them, but they were certainly present somewhere along the way in my visits during my period there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can Exhibit 576 be shown, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I'm going to tell you, sir, that this is a document of the Main Staff of the RSK army. This document was drafted towards the end of November 1992, and it is an order to form staffs and units of the Serbian army of the RSK. The date on the document is 27 November 1992. Now you have the document before you. Do you see it, please? This is an order of the Main Staff of the Serbian army, ordering the formation of staffs and units of the Serbian army. Do you have the document before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please turn to page 4? That's item 2.9. While we are waiting for the page to show up with item 2.9, item 2.9 speaks of the disbandment and reformation of the administration of special police units; B, 75th Special Police Units Brigade Knin, and the 92nd Special Police Units Brigade Benkovac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please look at page 6, item 3.10? Item 3.10 contains an order to disband and abolish the basic mobilisation plan for the 79th Brigade of special police units in Korenica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let's take a look at page 8. That's item 4.9. Item 4.9 contains an order to the effect that the basic mobilisation plan should be disbanded and abolished for the 80th Brigade of the special police units in Vojnic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please look at page 11, item 6.8 of the order? Before this comes up on the screen, let's say that this is the order to disband and abolish the basic mobilisation plan for the 85th Brigade of special police units in Okucani. That's the order under subitem A. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 13 of the document. Item 7.11 of the order, which contains an order to disband and abolish the basic mobilisation plan of the 87th Special Police Units Brigade in Vukovar and the 90th Brigade of Special Police Units in Beli Manastir. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with what I've just shown you, and that's a list of all the eight special police brigades you spoke of in connection with the chart we saw a moment ago, is it clear on the basis of this order that all of the eight brigades were disbanded and that their basic mobilisation plan was abolished? Does it clearly transpire from this order?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders do indicate that is what has been provided for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at chapter 2 on page 13 of the order. Chapter 2 of the order dated 27 November, which reads: "All previous establishments of the staffs and units of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the special police units of the Republic of Serbian Krajina are hereby revoked." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now look at item 4, under final provisions, which is on page 13 and continues through to page 14 of the document. Therefore, item 4 of the final provisions reads: "Special police brigades shall enter into the composition of the corps under whose area of responsibility they can be found and shall in every respect be subordinated to corps commanders as of 0001 hours on 1 December 1992." Do you see this item?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at item 6 of the record, which reads: "The Serbian army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina," which is actually established pursuant to this order, "shall keep and maintain its weapons and equipment in depots with the presence of UNPROFOR representatives," in brackets, they are invoking the UN plan for the peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia. Namely, item 15(C) of the plan. Do you see this particular portion of the order in item 6?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this order provided for the disbandment of special police brigades and their inclusion into the RSK army, and that they shall come under the command of the -- of corps starting from 1st December, does it therefore show that the chart that we saw of the police dated 29 November 1991, which talks of special police and states that it is under Martic's command, is it therefore clear that the chart is not consistent with what we have just seen in this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think the chart that my learned friend refers to admitted Exhibit 730 is dated 29 December 1992, and I think he mentioned 29th November 1991. So I think -- I think that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend. That's an error, definitely. The chart, Exhibit 730, is dated 29 December 1992. My question was put in connection with this particular correct date and I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documentation here does indicate an ending to the formalities of that grouping. However, our monitors on the ground encountered people who were armed in contravention of the Vance Plan and that they regarded as the Milicija, so there were people there on the ground functioning. So while the policy may be there, the reality was there were people still in the areas carrying out functions that we regarded as Milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this answer you gave, can you tell us whether UNCIVPOL distinguished between a MUP and its members? That's to say, members of the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina and the Territorial Defence. Did you distinguish between members of the police and members of the TO on the ground, or was it quite irrelevant for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We go back to the Vance Plan, where we were left with the local police providing a component with responsibility for policing, and it is that grouping of people that we referred to as Milicija. And again I don't think we differentiated between them in that sense but we certainly had them regarded as Milicija. They were presented as that. And that is how we responded and dealt with them in our reports, and they were there carrying out what would be regarded as a continuous function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The question was, though, did you distinguish between the members of the police and the members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. You have to get down to the nitty-gritty of answering that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Vance Plan left us with just a policing component within the mission, and we were aware that there were people there who were not police who had what we regarded as effectively a police uniform, police-type uniform. Our monitors reported that they had seen these people in other uniforms carrying out duties within the UNPAs. They knew them to see. They recognised them, but they saw them with other uniforms on occasions. So it's a question of what do you call them. What -- they regarded them as people who were part of the Milicija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at document from the 65 ter list, 344, in connection with this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we have the document on the screen, I would like to tell you that this is UNCIVPOL report dated 7 February 1993, and could we please see page 2 of the document? That's in B/C/S. I will give you the number. 65 ter document 344. I don't think we have the document. This is 65 ter document 344, an UNCIVPOL report. 344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could we get some help with getting it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, in case it assists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I believe Ms. Valabhji is trying to assist you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I think it's admitted Exhibit 740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. You have the number now. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is an UNCIVPOL report. Do you recognise it? It's been already before you. Could we turn to page 2, please, bearing the reference number R0426326? On this page, we have the situation report number 4, which speaks of the murder of husband and wife Palinic and can be found referred to in your statement. In the middle of this passage, it is stated that the local police arrested one suspect and that he was a member of the border police, and in brackets we have the abbreviation TDF, which is Territorial Defence force. I'd like to know the following: Were members of the police and members of the Territorial Defence one and the same thing to UNCIVPOL representatives?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that situation is expressed as member of the border Milicija, and these people fell -- remained within that grouping, as far as our monitors were concerned on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, let me remind you of the document you saw a moment ago concerning the disbandment and abolition of the basic mobilisation plan of special police units and their transformation into the army and their subordination to commanders of corps of the RSK army. In light of such a document, can you regard a member of the TO a police officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- our monitors on the ground functioned within the Vance Plan concept, and the people who were to be there policing the area were the Milicija. And those who were there were regarded as that. I know that the formalities of the documentation would indicate clearly that things had changed at an organisational level, but on the ground, we believe that nothing had changed, that the same people were there carrying out similar functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was your understanding of the situation. Thank you. I do not wish to dwell on this any further. We will go back to paragraph 29 of your statement, where you speak of trends, to the effect that the special police were actively intimidating Croats. That's under title "Expulsion of Croats from RSK." And one of the documents underlying this conclusion of yours is the 65 ter document 345. Could we please have that document on our monitors? 65 ter document, therefore. This is an UNCIVPOL report, Sector South, dated 8 February 1993. We have the document on our screens. Mr. McElligott, do you recognise the document? I believe we've seen it already.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is an UNCIVPOL Sector South document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could the registrar please move the document up a bit to -- in order to see the bottom of the document and the text itself? And Mr. McElligott, could you read the first paragraph under 3, operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the paragraph commencing with the date, is that correct, the 8th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is reported that the head of patrol in the village of Vrpolje, they met local Milicija who were guarding the residents of this village, the Croatians who were forced to leave their house by the refugees were still living in the school," I take it, "the Milicija informed CIVPOL that they have three buses to transport Croatians, people from the village, but they didn't get the confirmation from Sibenik that the CSI is ready to accept them. There was no complaints from those Croatian people during the visit." Do you wish me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no. Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Could we please move to page 350, or ending in numbers 350? I believe that's page 4 of the document. Not 351 but 350. This is a rather long report where, after that introductory part that you read out to us, again the topic of the refugees from Vrpolje is dealt with. Could you please read the second paragraph in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNCIVPOL patrols are being carried out in Knin itself, from Knin station. A common problem at present is that the local Croats are still being forced out of their houses and apartments by both newly arriving refugees and local opportunists. Local authorities appear powerless to stop this. Civil affairs is not participating in any plan to evacuate the over 260 persons to the Croatian side at present and instead is pressurising local authorities to deal with the problem. These authorities have been saying that no one will be expelled from their homes in this manner. Local authorities say that they will put these people back into their homes and flats. However, these people who are presently living in a small school, which is grossly overcrowded, with inadequate sanitary facilities refuse to move, and they are indicating to be transferred to the other side. Croatian authorities have rejected this. The situation here is worsening with a few more local Croats joining their numbers with each passing day."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. This is the report dated 8 February 1993. Let me remind you that on the 21st of January, or, rather, the 22nd of January, the large Croatian offensive against Maslenica was launched, and this report speaks of refugees that are arriving and forcing Croats from their houses. That's what we were able to read in the first paragraph. Basically these were refugees that were driven away from their homes by the Croatian army and, in retaliation, were in turn forcing Croats out of their homes. Here we have mention of refugees and local opportunists, and it is stated that local authorities were powerless in preventing this. Is that correct? Is this what you have just read out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that was the fallout of the 21st of January, that there was a push forward and people were displaced and moved on and displaced others, and I recall that being the situation that arose from the 21st or the 21st of January incursion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. McElligott, that this document is quite unlikely to lead to the conclusion that you drew in paragraph 29, that trends from these reports indicate that the special police were intimidating Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Just to point out that the witness was asked to read one paragraph of the report that's before us. I don't believe -- I'm not sure if he's seen this whole document, and the question that's being now put to the witness by my learned colleague is basing itself on the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? In relation to that response that you're going large?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to hear the witness's answer, keeping in mind the situation concerning the expulsion of Croats from Vrpolje and I wanted to see whether this case involved the special police or not. This was a group of Croat residents who were put up in a school, and this is something that we were faced with quite frequently during testimony, and the general assertion was that this was done by the special police. I wanted to hear from the witness whether in this case the Croats that were driven away from Vrpolje and placed in the school were in fact driven out of their homes by the special police or not and to draw a conclusion from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a single incident, Your Honour, and I know it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please do not go on with your evidence quite as yet. We are dealing with issues between the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- Requires patience. One moment, please. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Just to point out, Your Honour, this is not one of the documents that were discussed in the direct exam. I don't think it's been admitted. Again, I just reiterate what I said earlier, the point is that the document consists of several pages but only a portion has been made familiar to the witness at this time. So perhaps in fairness the witness needs to be shown the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic, if you're going to be asking the witness to draw conclusions on the entire document, whereas you have been just specific in your question, then you have to be fair to the witness and let him have the opportunity to be advised as to the entirety. That is the basic direction. So please follow accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will follow your guidance. I note that the document deals with a number of other issues that have nothing to do with the topic I was examining the witness on. This is about a number of UNCIVPOL stations which, due to the ongoing Maslenica operation, had to cease operating, and I simply picked out the parts that were relevant to me, just as the Prosecution is used to doing when examining. If you believe that I should have the witness read out the entire document, then I will withdraw the last question that I put to the witness, by your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Not the entire document but the entire relevant portions to your cross-examination within the guidelines, of course. Try and keep within the guidelines and go to him directly on relevant matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me just verify whether I have understood you correctly. Does the Trial Chamber accept the fact that I withdrew my last question, or do you insist on me presenting the whole document to the witness? I don't know whether I have understood your guidance well or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm trying to get you to understand it. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next chapter in your statement before paragraph 30 is entitled "Damage to Croatian villages and property (homes in RSK)." Amongst other things, in paragraph 33, when you're talking about these things, you say: "From my own observations, I recall that Croatian villages and communities in RSK were extensively damaged and abandoned." In this regard I would like to know whether you can tell us which village in Croatia was extensively damaged and abandoned during your tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ate this stage, Your Honour, I do not recall the specifics of villages. But when I went to areas I went on patrol generally with a station commander and I got a briefing from them and was shown and areas were identified to me. And there were houses and -- number of houses as described damaged and some of them put beyond inhabitation. So at this stage I cannot name a specific village, but I certainly saw them, and they were identified to me as Croatian little hamlets or villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I don't know whether you have understood me correctly. I am not disputing the fact contained in your statement that you were there, that you saw some houses and some villages that indeed were damaged. However, my question was whether there were any villages during your term of duty, while you were a member of the UNCIVPOL, that were damaged or abandoned. I'm talking about the villages that were damaged during the time you were there, during your tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I refer to the various reports and particularly the report submitted in -- by Inspector Noonan, from Sector South, and it refers to houses being damaged, and I think that would be the basis of information available to me. And I suppose follow-up to that would be when I went out on the ground, I went and looked at areas and saw for myself that there was extensive damage, but the overall report and indeed the same would prevail for reports coming in from the other sectors too. This report just deals with Sector South, but you would have a similar profile in other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, you testified based on Exhibit 721 that the authority of the UNCIVPOL was to observe the work of the local police in order to prevent for non-discrimination and to provide for the protection of human rights. Did you only observe the treatment of the Croatian population in the areas of protection or the overall population in those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our monitors patrolled the entire area of the protected areas and indeed they were very much in contact with the communities. I suppose the reality of it was that they lived within the communities and indeed most of them lived with Serbian people in the community, so that they were in touch with all sides and were conscious of incidents of all kinds, and all matters coming to their notice would be reported and were reported, and if incidents relating to Serb damages came to their notice they would be reflected in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Could you please be briefer in your answers in order to save time. On Friday, Exhibit 726 was shown to you and it was entitled "Crimes against Croats in Sector South." As I was reading the document, I could see that the document lists a number of incidents, including the theft of food, the theft of cattle. In your view, were all incidents that happened and were described in that report are all ethnically biased and committed only because the aggrieved parties were Croats, or do you maybe think that there was another motive to some of these incidents and crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at the entire grouping of crimes, and I recall you could brake them down into a group where the perpetrators were identified as people wearing what would be regarded as people in uniform, and then there was another breakdown where specific reference was made to Milicija uniform, and I think the covering note would suggest that the overall figure in that range is about 120. Now, there is another group, then, where you have suspects described as wearing civilian clothes and armed, and I think those figures are quite low. And there is another group, then, where you have people who are unarmed and in civilian attire, identified as suspects. Now, if I recollect correctly, there could be perhaps 25 to 30 per cent of the overall grouping where there is no suspect whatsoever identified. In other words, there is no evidence to indicate who perpetrated the crime. So I think that's kind of a broad breakdown of the overall situation. And where suspects are profiled I've -- the report indicates that 120 of those are in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a result of your answer, and I asked you specifically whether you believed that the theft of food, cattle, household appliances, and we are talking about numerous incidents of the sort, were these incidents motivated by the ethnicity of the aggrieved parties? You've answered I am not going to insist, although I believe that your answer was only partial. Many UNCIVPOL reports say that the complete Serb population was armed because of the Croatian attacks, all the Serbian males were armed because of that. Do you remember those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are reports to indicate there was a high level of arms. And I think in the breakdown of that report you will see where suspects are in civilian attire and armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. It's enough. Do you exclude the possibility that a soldier might also be hungry? And would you exclude such a circumstance as a possible motive for a crime?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if the report you have is one of a theft from somebody, that is a crime, and the fact that you are a soldier or otherwise doesn't exonerate you committing that crime, and indeed I think if you look at the victims, and many of them they are quite elderly people, so I don't rationalise it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did UNCIVPOL draft reports on crimes committed against other ethnic groups; for example, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All incidents coming to our notice were recorded. I know that this report specifically focused on the victims who were Croats, but all the other ones are recorded. I'm not sure if they are actually profiled in a single -- organised into a single document at this stage, but that is one that was prepared at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the UNPROFOR? Did UNPROFOR fall victim of the sudden theft of vehicles, parts of their vehicles, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, some vehicles were stolen. Radios were stolen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The information about crimes against Croats, was it compared with the general crime situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from looking at the situation reports, that the high level of victims were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you travelled a lot in order to perform your duties, that you travelled through Sector South and Sector North. Did you get an insight into the economic situation in those areas? Was there enough electricity, food, water? Was there any electricity or water at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no electricity. I think on occasions you might have electricity at a weekend or water at a weekend, and I had stayed with families, Serbian families in the Knin area when I went there, and there was no electricity. I have recollections of the lady in the house baking her loaf of bread outdoors on the fire, and at night we sat with a candle and the loaf of bread and a leg of prosciutto, and that was our social night, and indeed I would say a very social night, a very friendly -- and one I will always remember. And I think our monitors are very, very conscious of how people lived, because they lived with them and lived it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Before the break, I'm going to show you a document. The numbers R006-812, and R006-825. Before we see the document on the screen -- is the document on the screen? Can the registry confirm that this is the document that I called for? Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see it on my screen. Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The number is R006-8012-R006-8025. Before the document appears on the screen, on page 6, in paragraph 3 of this report, it says, and you're going to see the paragraph in a minute: "The collapse of order and law in many parts of the former Yugoslavia and the struggle for survival of the local population have created the atmosphere that the special commission for the investigation of the situation considers to be conducive to -- for illegal activities geared for personal gain. This applies to the local population as a well as to members of the international organisations. At this moment, at least 56 organisations are accredited through the UNHCR." I called for this document so as to be able to read this paragraph of this report, and if you're agreeable, Your Honours, I believe that we'll be able to go -- to go on looking through the document after the break. I believe this is the convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You would like to take the break now and then we look at the document and then you continue on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. This is precisely what I have told you, to keep to our timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. The registrar will locate the document in the interim and we get it on the system. Thank you so much. Can we take our adjournment now until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, my last question was about the economic situation and you spoke about problems with water, electricity and so on and so forth. I tried to show you a document, and it seems that I created a problem and the registry could not help me with that. I recorded a wrong number, so I won't insist on this document being shown. I'll try and reach an answer through my verbal question without the assistance of any documents. Given your insight into the situation on the ground, Mr. McElligott, could you say that the collapse of law and order in many parts of the former Yugoslavia, as well as the struggle for the survival of the local population, created an atmosphere which might have been conducive to illegal activities geared for personal gain? You're an experienced police officer, and I would like to know whether you can possibly answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that an environment of this nature would generate I suppose a different type of crime, I suppose. One would look at what could be an organised crime in the sense that you introduce black market, and I think there could be issues relating to currency and exchange rates and this type of thing. They arise in the middle of this environment, and certainly there were areas of that or issues like that taking place certainly, and I think it also went down to I suppose what would be the theft of very basic items, too, because of very low supply of even food at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. As a professional, do you believe that such an economic situation contributed to a large extent to the rise in crime rates? I believe that you've already answered that question, but I would like to hear it again more directly from you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were thefts, like the profile of the crime even in this report does show the theft of some very basic things; indeed, yesterday was reference was made to the theft of timber from a particular house. So I think the very elementary types of crime were committed, but behind that there were very serious crimes committed, and we have profiled murders, murders of families. So there is a dividing line. There is what I suppose ordinary petty crime, perhaps based at times on the absolute needs of some people, but then there is another profile running as well that has a whole different dimension to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this would be my question to you: How to understand this issue of raising -- of rising crime rates in this period, in this region. This is a very general question, and could you specify what types of crime you mean, you're referring to? Do you have any special statistics on crime rates you're referring to? Or how else should we understand your question or the gist of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't want to go into any details of this topic. I just wanted to hear the witness's position and his knowledge about the general situation on the ground during that period, given a large number of reports that speak about the theft of bare essentials. If this becomes a recurrence, and if this strikes certain groups of people, certain parts of the population, it may have an impact. What I wanted to know is whether the overall situation lended itself to higher crime rates. I got an answer, which I was happy, but if the Honourable Judges think that the topic should be elaborated, I am only too happy to do that. I might be able to do that. My question was relative to a general situation. It was a principal question. That's why I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I see it's a principal question, and it was also answered in a very principal way. And I was wondering if this really would satisfy, because this doesn't express anything specific concerning the different fields of the crime statistics at that time, at that period. But if you don't mean it in a special way, then we can leave it like that. I'm fine with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic, unless you have something further to respond to Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No. I'm happy with the answer I got and with the way that the question was tackled. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's now deal with the issue of UNCIVPOL stations. You spoke about the functioning of those stations that existed on the ground in all UNPA areas. Can Defence Exhibit number 1D0042 be shown, please? Before we see the report on the screen, I'll tell you, Mr. McElligott, that this is an UNCIVPOL report for Sector South, for July 1993. During this short break, I'm going to tell you that this is a report containing an additional report for June 1993, and this is an overview of incidents per stations. Have you got the document before you, Mr. McElligott?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask to which number you refer, by saying 042, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave you the whole number. This is number 1D0042, a Defence Exhibit, 1D0042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Milovancevic, did you say June of 1993? A report containing a report in relation to June 1993? Because I don't see that on the document that is before me. And your colleague, learned counsel for the OTP, is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm told that this might be 1D00-1789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji. Mr. Milovancevic, you've been given assistance as to the location of your Defence exhibit. Could we try and get it up on the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I would also like to thank my learned friend. I have the hard copy of the document. This is a report of the civil police of Sector South, which is relative to the monthly report of Sector South for July 1993. The number on it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the counsel could repeat that number slowly, it would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think it's 1D00-1789. And perhaps the ERN might facilitate things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milovancevic repeat the number? The interpreter did not catch the number that Mr. Milovancevic was quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, could you repeat the number which you were quoting, for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is Defence Exhibit 1D0042. And this is a monthly report of the UNCIVPOL for July 1993, and on its first page, this is the document on the screen, this is the document on the screen, thank you very much. I apologise for the misunderstanding. I don't understand what the problem is, but I know that my learned friend has tried to assist me and I thank her for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document, that is before you now, Mr. McElligott, and I apologise once again for this waste of time, do you recognise this document as an UNCIVPOL document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this title page, do you know who drafted it, who the addressee is, and what is the date that it is bearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to the commissioner of UNCIVPOL and it's from sector chief UNCIVPOL Sector South. It is dated -- or it's end of month report for UNCIVPOL Sector South, July 1993. Is there a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have page 5 on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did you not want the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this is a monthly report, as far as I can see, there is no date on the cover page, but by reviewing the document, we'll establish the date, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we take a look at page 5 of the document? You have before you page 5 of the document. Could you please read the title on this page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a supplementary month end report for June 1993, breakdown of incidents by station. And then the first one mentioned is Vrlika, zone A, pink zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The document on this page indicates that the UNCIVPOL station at Vrlika was evacuated on the 23rd of January, 1993, whereas the Drnis station on the 27th of January. Do you know why the stations were evacuated? Was the reason for it the Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 23rd of January, I know that Benkovac incident arose somewhere there, was 22nd, 23rd. Perhaps this was a further fallout of that. Off the top of my head, I don't recall the detail, but certainly I remember the Benkovac one, and that was early -- or mid-January or late January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 6 on the screen, with -- bearing the number 647 at the top right-hand corner? On this page, it is indicated that the Bratiskovski, Smokovic, Medak and Teslingrad stations were evacuated in late January 1993. Does the same apply to these stations, your statement concerning the Drnis and Vrlika stations, that in fact they were evacuated during the Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an evacuation of a number of stations, yeah, and I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did UNCIVPOL have access to these locations after the Maslenica operation? Do you recall these details?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a delay in getting back into these areas for a period of time. I think that is even referred to here at the top of the report in relation to - is it Vrlika? - that they are managing to get some patrols in from Knin at that stage in June. So there was -- like they didn't get back to base for sometime, but the top of the report would suggest they were getting patrols in there on a limited basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Could we take a look at page 8, the last three numbers are 4 -- 649. You will see that on page 8, it is stated that the UNCIVPOL station from Benkovac was relocated to Knin on 29 January 1993 and that monitors go to their station from Knin every morning. Do you know why the UNCIVPOL station was relocated from Benkovac? Was the reason the same as the one that applied to the stations we saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Benkovac, I know that on the morning of the incursion, at 20 -- that one or two of our monitors were taken hostage and held on the top floor of the hotel there for a number of days, and they were eventually negotiated out and returned to Knin. Now, at that stage, our monitors did not return to the area because they were, as I say, they were held hostage for a period of time and they eventually got to patrol the area and basing themselves in Knin, so the entire station party was actually taken hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you seem to remember this event, do you recall this happening at the time when Croatia launched its attack on an UNPA zone? Was that the same period of time as when this particular event occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember Benkovac specifically. I was there that night. So I have a clear recollection of the situation in the morning, and I left that day, and subsequent to that our monitors were held for a number of days, so I was eventually involved in negotiating their release. So I have a specific recollection of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, you didn't tell me whether this took place at the time when the Croatian forces launched the Maslenica operation. Did this take place at the same point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the Maslenica operation to me earlier on and I'm not associating the name with a specific event, but certainly if you're tying it to the same day and the Benkovac scenario, this is the one I recall clearly in the sense there was an incursion by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Who was it who held those officers in hostage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were under the control of the local Milicija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they -- it -- the area was very much a battlefield, I suppose, or a fully operational military field at that point. There was quite a lot of what you call Serbian response in the area. I believe that quite a lot of the military could also have been based in the hotel, but the police were the people specifically holding our people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this page it is stated that the Obrovac UNCIVPOL station was also evacuated on the 21st of January, 1993, and that its operations were relocated to Kistanje. This station, just as all the previous ones in Benkovac, Bratiskovski, Smokovici, Medak, Teslingrad, Vrlika and Drnis, was evacuated in the second half of January 1991, after the start of the Maslenica operation. Do you tie this evacuation up with the combat activities taking place at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a whole fallout following the Benkovac situation and I suppose the mission went into turmoil basically at that point, certainly down at the Sector South end of it. And I think that is reflected there, that we had to draw back from a lot of our stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. We will move on to a different topic, although it is connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There is an objection being taken by Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, not an objection but just to say that in the question posed, the second half of January 1991 is being referred to and I think that's a mistake. Should be 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you accept that it was an error?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I thank my learned friend. It was a slip of the tongue. Of course the year was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McElligott, I'm going to ask you about quite a different topic. We are still on page 8 of the document. Could you please read out the first two lines of the second paragraph below the title "Benkovac"? Which starts with the following words "Benkovac was shelled." So I'm interested in the first two lines.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- where about it is? Yeah. "Benkovac was shelled on the 1st of the 7th, 1993, 2nd of the 7th, 1993, the 13th of the 7th, 1993, the 14th of the 7th, 1993, the 15th of the 7th, 1993. utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, like at this stage, not off the top of my head but I'm aware that there were serious incidents where the escalation of the conflict rose to that level where shelling was undertaken. I was quite -- yes, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of the document, bearing the last numbers 643 on the screen? Please read out the first four sentences immediately below the title "3. Operations," which starts with the following words: "The overall situation in this sector is..." Could you please read out the first four sentences?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The overall situation in this sector is tense. Most of the sector experienced shelling for the week prior to the 18th of the 7th, 1993. No injuries to CIVPOL personnel were reported across the sector as a" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McElligott, as was the case with the shelling of Benkovac, where wheat-fields were mentioned, do you agree that here it was quite evident that the Croatian artillery was firing upon the inhabited areas within an UNPA, and these were areas predominantly inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have page 5 of the document on the screen, bearing the last numbers 646? utterances.text: I don't know. Well, I accept that if the shelling took place in the -- from the outside the UNPA it's going to be the Croatian authorities who are doing it. I don't know who -- it doesn't say there who took anything. So again, I think when -- again when you go back to the report, the overall report, it does say that we did lack information for a period of time in a number of stations, so there is a gap, and while there is a theft there from Croatian, it doesn't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. That will do. You have provided a detailed answer. In addition -- and I apologise for interrupting you. I do not mean disrespect but merely want to save time. At the very start of my cross-examination, we were referring to operation Medak pocket. In connection with this, and given that this was an UNPA area and that the Croatian army attacked the area at the time when you were out in the field, I would like to show you Defence document 1D0032 before putting my question to you. I hope I'll have more luck with the numbers now than I had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What are you going to do in respect of the other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since that's a Defence Exhibit, I believe it's already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is not the case, I will subsequently move that it be done, but based on the records I have here, it seems to be a Defence Exhibit. By your leave, I would like to proceed and then we could deal with that at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document? Can you tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of it is, as I write over it, like a covering note across the report but it contains Cedric Thornberry's signature. Is that the one you're showing me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who drafted the document, who it was addressed to and which date it bears? Can you see that on the page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- there is a cover --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. To facilitate the proceedings, we will move to page 2. I made a mistake by indicating this particular page which is quite illegible. Could we move to page 2, please? utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is addressed to the first commander for the information of the SLSG and the DFC and it's from the Cedric -- signed by Cedric Thornberry, NCA, dated the 3rd of October, 1993, and the subject is "report on Medak events."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you maybe repeat once more from whom it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was from -- from -- is it the HC -- is it HC? And signed Cedric Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Could we now have page 19 of the document on our screen, bearing the number 356? These are the last three digits. When we have the page on our screens, could you please read paragraph 48, under title "recommendation"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR has conducted a systematic investigation of conditions in the Medak area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I would just raise at this time the objection on the basis of relevance, Your Honour. If this is going to be about crimes committed by the opposing side, what is the relevance? I had raised this objection yesterday, and I think my learned friend in his response referred to his desire to pursue the line of questioning concerning the role of the United Nations. I think this is now going beyond that. So I just -- I object on this basis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me hear your response. The Trial Chamber is interested to hear what you have to say in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the situation is relatively simple for the Defence. Mr. McElligott, having been a high official of UNCIVPOL, and as he is testifying in relation to the period of time while he was out in the field, in leading this piece of evidence, the Defence wishes to see whether the way the witness presented the situation was complete and objective, whether it represents what happened on both sides, and whether the matters he presents are in fact imbedded in the context at the time or not. To the Defence, every crime is a crime, and we believe that the fact that some mass-scale military operations were carried out at the time can have an impact on the general situation in the area. That is why the Defence was pursuing this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just respond very briefly that I recall that the witness was already asked about his visit to the area subsequent to the operation, and he's already responded on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In so far -- Mr. Milovancevic? In so far that it might relate to the issue of credibility, we are going to allow you to pursue it in a very limited fashion, to explore the issue of balance and objectivity in relation to the account that is given by the witness thus far, but please keep it very straight and within the confines of what I've placed before you. Are you hearing me? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand, and I have only one question to put to the witness on this matter. And I am aware of the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, although the paragraph is rather longish, I'd appreciate it if you read it out.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. "UNPROFOR has conducted a systematic investigation of conditions in the Medak area and the events described in the report show that the Croatian army attack in the area on the 9th of September was fully coordinated and planned. It met little or no Serb resistance. Croatian troops killed most of those who were unable to make good their escape, regardless of age, sex or status, and a number are still missing. Massive destruction to property was conducted by the Croatian forces during their events and particularly during their withdrawal. Virtually all houses and outbuildings in the villages and surrounding hamlets were destroyed, many by explosion. Wells were destroyed or damaged. Household chattels were deliberately destroyed and almost all remaining domestic animals were killed. During a period in which UNPROFOR personnel were prevented from moving into the area in accordance with a prior agreement with the Croatian army, the destruction was completed. UNPROFOR members hearing explosions and shooting and shortly after observing houses in ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down with the reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... in flames. Thus, a comprehensive scorched earth policy was practised by the Croatian army. While the commanding officer, officer in charge of the Croatian army in this undertaking are not identified in this report, these details are available. It is recommended that the report be transmitted to the special rapporteur for human rights commission and to the acting chairman of the Commission of Experts on war crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. One question on this issue. Based on your knowledge, after having toured the area, would you agree with the description of the events as you read them out now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on this subject. I'd like to know whether during your term of service, UNCIVPOL conducted investigations into some other crimes committed by the Croatian forces against Serb civilians. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made reference to one in my direct evidence, if I can recall, and it was -- could you, sir, can I have your question again? In relation to attacks on Serbs? Yes. Civilians. Yes. That's the one I made reference to during my direct evidence, and when I examined a particular period of time, in relation to the complaint, I established that the Croatians had killed a number of Serb civilians in excess of those on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can Exhibit 1D0035 be shown, please? To be more precise, it's page 2, please. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can page 2, please, be shown? The last three digits are 203. You can see that you authored this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And who the addressee was and what is the indication of the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is addressed to Cedric Thornberry through the commissioner, and it is dated the 24th of February, 1993. And the subject is alleged mass graves between Poljane and Pakrac on and GAJ Sector West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the first paragraph and the first two sentences of the second paragraph? The first paragraph begins with the words the attached report from Sergeant Nicholson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: MS. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise yet again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: But I have to return, I'm afraid, to my objection on the basis of relevance. I think now this really goes beyond the very limited scope of questioning pertaining to other crimes, and I would also recall in this context the Trial Chamber's guidelines on the Tu Quoque defence, the fact that the Tribunal does not recognise it as a valid defence and has accepted only to a very limited extent evidence relating to crimes allegedly committed by other parties to the conflict. And in this regard, I would recall the Kupreskic trial judgement which I believe is referred to in the guidelines as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, can we hear from you in response to learned counsel for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In regard to this document, the Defence has just one question. That's the first explanation. And the second explanation is my response to the objection. And that is that it would really be pointless to use the Tu Quoque defence. However, what is important for the Defence at the moment is what ground among what people and into which territory the UNPROFOR forces and the civil police arrived. The problem on the ground did not start on the 2nd of October, 1992 when Mr. McElligott joined the CIVPOL. It had started much earlier, and the Defence would like to demonstrate that these problems on the ground that had a direct bearing on the behaviour and the position of the overall population regardless of their ethnicity had existed much longer before and that they had already been dealt with by UNCIVPOL. If this is not important, the question arises how come that UNCIVPOL that arrived in 1992 launched investigations into the matters that were topical in 1990 and 1991. When this report was drafted the UNCIVPOL thought this was very important for the overall situation and for the assessment of the possible behaviour of the international forces towards the civilian population as well as vice versa. In that sense, I'm trying to present my case, and I am not in any case attempting to engage in the Tu Quoque defence. It would really be unprecedented and pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Forgive me for making this observation, but it appears this is the direction you're heading in. Could you encapsulate your objections within the framework that is necessary? Because you have said, in effect, that you are not pursuing Tu Quoque, but what is the purpose specifically? Please encapsulate what you're saying because you seem to ramble somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only one question on this topic should demonstrate that the complete population in the territory where the UNPA areas were and where the civilian police was deployed, that the total population regardless of their religion or ethnicity was at risk due to the war activities that were going on at the time. All the population suffered and the general position on the ground determined the reactions of the population on all sides, or on both sides, regardless of their ethnicity. What I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now that is apparently the Defence case, part and parcel of the Defence case. That's the first thing that the Chamber would like to establish. Right. Let us hear what your question will be. The witness is asked not to respond. The Chamber would like to hear what this question will be, within the framework of what you have said the Defence case is on this specific point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question will be as follows: It will be just one and it will be relative only to whether the UNCIVPOL launched an investigation into the suffering of the people and how this arose, under what circumstances, and who was responsible for that population. Nothing else. That's all. This topic, in my further cross-examination, should have taken no more than a minute of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It's not a question of how much time. It's whether you are correct in the course that you're pursuing. First of all, the Chamber makes the observation that it sounds very much like more than one question, and within the framework that you have put it, it seems to go beyond what is permitted. And I'm going to rule that you not pursue this area. You're not permitted to. And you move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, there is no need for you to answer. You understood the Chamber's ruling. Let us now address an issue that is mentioned in some of the UNCIVPOL documents, only very briefly. Can document 1D0042 be shown? This is the UNCIVPOL report for June 1993.
