utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall ask for the admission of this document as a Defence exhibit. utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very well, please go ahead.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the one referring to freedom of movement; is that correct? No? An ongoing situation, sorry. "An ongoing situation has developed in Zaluznica on the 19th of the 7th, 1993. The next day the village threw up a roadblock demanding the release of their men. CIVPOL played a crucial role in defusing the situation several times over the period of 20th -- of July 20th of the 7th, 1993 to the 26th of 7, 1993. All efforts" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. McElligott. You're aware of this incident, aren't you? This was caused by the Croatian side in the area that was under your control?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can page 8 be displayed, bearing the last three digits 649? The same document. On this page, Mr. McElligott, when you have it before you, look at the middle of the page and can you start reading from the sentence starting with "one Serb soldier"? And when you're reading Mr. McElligott, could you please do it slowly for the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where exactly is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The second third of the text, towards the last paragraph. Towards the very end of the page, the last several sentences, before the last paragraph, the end of the previous paragraph. The text that I would like you to read starts -- no, no, no, no, stop, go back, go back, scroll down, scroll down, more. Stop. What I want you to read starts with the words "one Serb soldier." Below the table there is a long paragraph preceded by a short sentence. At the edge of that long paragraph, the fourth sentence line from the bottom starts with "one Serb soldier," or the fourth sentence from the bottom starts with the words "one Serb soldier." utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a sentence commencing with "local Milicija." Where is in relation to that sentence? Abducted soldier now -- okay. Yeah, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It's not very easy, Mr. McElligott. There is a lot of text. But this is the sentence that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One Serb soldier was abducted during a patrol along with two others, which were wounded in the encounter. Abducted soldier now POW - happened 15/07/1993. utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. Once again, I apologise for the difficulties this text posed. There is lots of it. Are you familiar with this and similar incidents which speak about the behaviour of the Croatian side towards the Serbs on the ground and towards the Serbian population as well as towards the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of those incidents, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just to give you a polite reminder that we have 15 minutes left before the close of this section, having regard to your statement before that you would finish cross-examination by the end of this session -- or by the middle of this session, I'm reminded. So you seem to have gone beyond your mark. I assume that you are near the end, very near, because we are near our next adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may need another five minutes. I would like to apologise. We've had some difficulty with displaying documents on the screen. I am approaching the end of my cross-examination and I will bear your words in mind. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard the situation on the ground in Sector South, where you have had the presence of the refugees, can document 1D0043 be shown, please? utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a CIVPOL report from Sector South. utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC

utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought it was on. My apologies are in order. Relevance at this stage? We are going wide again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm establishing a link between this document and the documents relative to Vrlika and Croatian population that had been expelled from their homes by the Serbian citizens that had been previously expelled by the Croatian army from some other areas. utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Hasn't the witness given that evidence before, generally? Why rehash it if it's not absolutely necessary and if it's causing you to breach the rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your suggestion, Your Honour. I'll move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Your five minutes is almost up as well. Please go along nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of all the things that we have discussed so far, through the questions put to you, Mr. McElligott, can one say, and I believe that this is going to be my last question to you, that during the period while you were a member of the mission, the area under the control of the United Nations was drastically attacked by the Croatian armed forces on several occasions around Maslenica, at least ten villages were leveled with the ground, a lot of people had been expelled from the Medak pocket where three villages were erased, and that many other places where there were attacks by Croatian artillery. There were other examples of incursions of up to 600 people from Croatia under arms into the territories under the control of the United Nations. Wouldn't it be evident from all this that the protection forces of the United Nations were failing in performing their mission that was envisaged by the Vance's plan to protect the entire population in those territories from attacks and from the terror?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all part of what was an ongoing conflict and certainly all those things mentioned took place. I think we have to reflect on what happened within the UNPAs as well, and that has to be taken into consideration. So it was a very tumultuous time. And that was the environment that those of us who were there had to work with. I suppose I would say as well that it goes back to the -- the police or the -- in the area with responsibility had to show leadership and strength to manage that conflict and to gain the confidence of those within. And I think that ongoing conflict, one was sparking the other, and I suppose it is very hard to put a balance to it, and I think this is where our role came into play and indeed the local police role came into play was stabilising the UNPAs and trying to gain the confidence of the community within it. And, you know, I said earlier that if that had happened, that perhaps a lot of the other things would not have happened, but again hindsight is a great thing. So that was the environment of the day, and I have no doubt it impacted on everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your last question, that was? And we wish to thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have indeed finished my cross-examination. I would like to thank Mr. McElligott. The cross-examination was rather long. A lot of it had to be read, but that was the nature of the matter. I would like to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Now, Ms. Valabhji, do you have any re-examination or redirect, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. I have a few questions. Before I commence, I was just wondering if my learned colleague intended to seek the admission of R0426642? I don't think it's in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What is your position, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to my learned friend for reminding me. Your Honour, the Defence has offered several documents for admission during the last session. I would like them to be admitted as Defence exhibits. The last document was 1D0042.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, we had 1D0042. I thought that it was admitted but it hasn't been admitted. This document is the one that has been interpreted by the witness and was relative to the UNCIVPOL police stations that had been evacuated in several places. I hope you remember the document. I may be a bit belated with the admission of this document. Please, I would like to apologise for thinking that the document has already been admitted. I was wrong. So can I seek its admission now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The document is duly admitted. Could an exhibit number be assigned to it in those circumstances, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to seek admission of the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're not asking for them to be admitted together? Because the registrar hasn't done that which is necessary as yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit number 742 will be assigned to 1D0043. 743 will be given to 1D0042.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me just look. If you could just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, could we do it step by step? You asked for admission of 1D0042, and so this was admitted and we asked for an exhibit number, only for this one. Final digits 42.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is 00743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And what is 742?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 742 is assigned to 1D0043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Was that already asked for --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 43 is given to 1D0042. Can I just repeat? Exhibit number 742 is assigned to the document 1D0043. Exhibit number 743 is assigned to the document 1D0042.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more thing. The last document that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You had not in fact made your application in respect of 43 as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for another document as well. In order to avoid any confusion, I would like to seek admission of 1043 and 1D0032. That was relative to the Medak pocket. I failed to do that, and those are the three documents that I seek admission of, and I apologise for the misunderstanding that I may be creating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask the first of the two, when was this discussed? 0043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think what has taken place is -- what had taken place is that I had mentioned that there was 0043 when he had specifically mentioned 0042. And he was in fact referring to the first one, and the registrar, I think, ran a little bit ahead of him and assigned for 43 when he had not had formally his application before the Trial Chamber. So having now placed his application before the Trial Chamber, what I will do is ask for an exhibit number to be assigned to it. Can we confirm the exhibit number assigned in it's duly accepted as an exhibit and we confirm the exhibit number assigned in respect of 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The registrar has explained that there is a formal application before the Trial Chamber. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just want to double-check whether 43 has been discussed in the direct -- in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It was discussed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It was not discussed or do you mean if he cross-examined in respect of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: If he cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My recollection is that he did, but could we check the record to ensure whether or not this is so?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We are running a little bit beyond the adjournment period. I ask for the indulgence of the interpreters and all officers of the court concerned, if we just get past this hurdle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm advised that it's at page 47, line 23 of the transcript, when the cross-examination in relation to this particular exhibit was placed on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think -- I wonder if the ERN might be mentioned here so that maybe it's easier. I'm still not sure if 43 was discussed at that point in the transcript or if we were still on 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji, Mr. Milovancevic, as it appears that the witness will have to return anyway, I'm going to propose that we take the adjournment now. We enquire into what has taken place in terms of the record in relation to this exhibit, and when we return at quarter to 6.00 then we can deal with it and ascertain properly what the position is and then take steps to either have it on the record as an exhibit or not, depending on what the record reveals. So could we take our adjournment now and return at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. I believe the record has now been checked. The transcript, that is. And the position ascertained in relation to the three documents, and in relation to Exhibit 1D0043, I was mistaken in the belief that it -- you were allowed to cross-examine on it. It was rejected on the grounds of relevance, I believe. And do you have anything to say in respect of the documents that you're putting forward now, having had the opportunity to see the record and the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I lent to the situation by my omission to tender documents on time. The document that should be admitted into evidence is 042, and 032, which is the document referring to Medak pocket. As for 043, we opened the document but the questions were not allowed, and that is why we will not tender it into evidence. But I do move that the other two documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think effectively one has already been admitted, and that is 1D0042. The Trial Chamber admitted that document and asked for an exhibit number to be assigned, and an exhibit number was assigned, which the registrar will confirm. Please confirm again for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The exhibit number is 743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We are very grateful to you. And then now in respect of this other one, which is 003 -- 0032. And you were asking for that one to be admitted also? Duly admitted by the Trial Chamber. Could an exhibit number be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There the exhibit number will be 742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that effectively dispose of the matter of the exhibits, Mr. Milovancevic, and I believe we can now ask Ms. Valabhji to re-examine, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a brief re-examination on two topics. Could 65 ter 333 please be displayed. This is admitted Exhibit 731. Could we just look at the paragraph under the heading "general overview"? And please scroll up so that we can see the title of the document. Great.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a number of questions about this document by the Defence. I will ask you one question about it right now. And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: This paragraph of the document refers to a stalemate and to both sides hardening their positions. It's not necessary to read allowed the whole paragraph. We can see it before us. My question is: Did this situation of stalemate and both sides hardening their positions, did that reflect the situation that you encountered when you arrived at CIVPOL in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a stalemate, and indeed I remember on days talking with the commissioner and expressing -- we expressed the view that if we could just make one person happy today or help one person today we would have achieved something, and I think it had got to absolutely going nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And my second topic is -- well, could 65 ter 349 please be displayed. Thank you. Sir, you were asked in cross-examination a number of questions pertaining to an end of month report from CIVPOL Sector South pertaining to July 1993, and with regard to this document, I'd like to ask you, in brief, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you narrow it slightly, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could it please be --

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report from Commissioner Michael O'Reilly, and at the top -- a little bit please, little further, to just to get to -- addressed to Mr. Thornberry, and it's dated the 14th of August, 1993, and the subject is attack on Croatian minorities in the Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Could we turn to page 5 of the document, which is the last page? And could you read aloud the third sentence which commences "cooperation from the..." until end of this paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cooperation from the local Milicija has waned" -- "Cooperation from the local Milicija has waned over the past week and with the increased shelling prior to the 18th of the 7th, 1993, a few contacts were possible. Since 18/7/1993, contact with the Milicija has decreased notably. We continue to request meetings with their representatives but are told that the people are busy or away performing other duties. I am attempting to contact the minister for the interior here in Knin to raise these issues with him. And I am hopeful that more beneficial contacts will resume." And that is from one of the investigating officers in Sector South, Steve Marissink.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is duly admitted. Could an exhibit number be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be 744.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Hoepfel, do you have any questions to ask of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have just a couple of questions that I'd like to pose to the witness. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what exactly was UNCIVPOL supposed to do in protecting the UNPAs, what was their real role?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our role was one of monitoring the activities of the local police and that was the central role that we did have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you something following on from that. Now, having received a report and then forwarding the report to the Milicija, if you did not get a response and say in the case of Mr. Martic, when you made the contents of a report known to him and asked for his response in the matter, having not got a response, under those circumstances, was there UN protocol or a CIVPOL protocol as to how that lack of response should be dealt with by CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: CIVPOL reported to civil affairs, and the protests were, in general, made through civil affairs. They dealt with what would be the political element of the mission. So generally you will see a report or a protest made through Mr. Thornberry and followed through would come at that level, at political level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. So what I'd like to find out, what the Trial Chamber would like to find out, at that level, from your knowledge what system was in place to address coming up against a lack of response.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that these matters would be raised at other levels in the mission, at -- again, the force commander, when he was head of the mission, would pursue matters at other levels, so that if there was no response coming, we felt that there was no response, but the matter would be raised at other levels in the system, so I would feel that there was always pursuit, perhaps to the highest level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And who would that highest level be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be -- well, I think at one stage we ended up with the Secretary-General's representative in the mission, and I expected that the protests would go through at, let's put it, UN level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my next question, it's in relation to the Vance Plan and the extract which we saw. Now, what I want to know from you is there a full record or full copy of the Vance Plan, or a copy of the full Vance Plan is really the correct description.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a document available, yes, I remember there being one available to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did you have that copy of the full Vance Plan? Do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a copy now, no. But there was one available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would learned counsel for either the OTP or the Defence have any questions arising out of the questions from the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: From Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I want to thank you for coming. The Trial Chamber is very grateful to you for your patience and that is the end of your evidence. You'll be pleased to hear that we will say goodbye to you now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji, do you have an application to make to me now, I suppose, as is customary?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right. May I be excused? Ms. Richterova will be handling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I will consult with the other member of the Trial Chamber to see if we can excuse you. Please excuse us. The answer is in the affirmative, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm most grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate how you recognised the tight rein that I hold over other counsel. Your Honour, the next witness will be handled by Ms. Valabhji, and if that witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Richterova. The witness is Charles Kirudja. While the witness is being brought in and Ms. Richterova is changing her seat, I'm wondering if I could raise a matter with respect to the length of cross-examinations of witnesses? Just very briefly. I know it's been raised at specific instances during cross-examinations. I'd like to address it in a broader sense. And we are extremely concerned about this pattern of extremely long and overlong and unjustifiably long cross-examinations. The last -- I've just reviewed the last five or six witnesses, and the cross-examinations in all those cases have far exceeded the direct examinations of the witnesses. In this last case, the witness was examined in direct for two sessions, under two sessions. He was cross-examined for five sessions. Now, if the -- if there were -- if there was a reason for such a lengthy cross-examination, then that would be fine, and the Defence is entitled to have the time that is required to make his defence. However, in our submission, that has -- that's been far from the case. The cross-examinations have been unduly long for a variety of reasons, all of which I think have been recognised by the Court, excessively long questions which contain summary of positions, summary of documents, and argument. Secondly, a number of irrelevant questions, which go far beyond the proper scope of cross-examination and go into matters which are not relevant to the charges. Third, reading documents into the record. And also going over documents that are already in evidence and simply making argument about them, using the cross-examination to simply argue to the Court or to the witness about documents or matters that are already in the record, and it's unnecessary. That can be done in final submissions. In our submission, this -- I mean, we are paid to do this job whether we are sitting in court, whatever. It's not a huge burden on the lawyers to sit. However, it is an enormous burden on the system and on the pace of this trial. It's prolonging the length of this trial, to the point where it almost seems like a deliberate strategy to prolong the length of the trial. And perhaps that's going too far, but it's getting to that point where we are beginning to feel that way. But that's not the most important thing. This is -- it's very difficult to schedule witnesses. We've had witnesses sitting here waiting to testify for a very long time. It's enormously inconvenient to them. It's also, I would submit, unfair to the witnesses who are being cross-examined for that length of time and in that manner, with repetitive, lengthy sometimes very general questions. And it's just making it very difficult to run this trial. We would ask for two -- that this be addressed in two ways by the Trial Chamber. First, we would ask that the Trial Chamber's guideline about the length of cross-examination be specifically enforced in the following manner: That at the beginning of the cross-examination, the Defence -- the Defence counsel either agree -- he either agrees that the cross-examination will not exceed the length of the direct examination, or makes an application at that time to the Trial Chamber for a longer period of time for cross-examination and explains why that is necessary in that particular case. And then it will -- and then it is then decided how much longer time will be granted. The -- Defence counsel has in the previous -- with the previous witness suggested that the number of documents that the witness introduced was a justification for a longer cross-examination. I would respectfully disagree. The documents are in evidence, and I would submit that many of the cross-examination questions were merely argument about the documents and no real information was elicited about the documents which were already in evidence, so I think that was unnecessary. So we would ask that that procedure be followed to try to get control over this process and to allow us to be able to plan more effectively how long things are going to take, so that we do not have witnesses waiting here unnecessarily. Secondly, I would ask the Court this week, so that we may be able to catch up a little bit, to consider sitting some extra time on Friday in the morning. I've raised this with the Defence counsel, and for a variety of reasons Defence counsel opposes this request. However, when I raised it, I think I raised it in the context of sitting the entire day on Friday, the full morning and the full afternoon. Perhaps we could consider not sitting the entire day but perhaps sitting an extra session in the morning, so that, as I said, we may be able to start to catch up a little bit because we are falling behind here or our witnesses, and now we have witnesses waiting for days to testify. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, without pre-empting what the ruling would be in relation to this, or a decision, would there be an available courtroom for the extra hours, or is -- am I thinking prematurely in asking to you respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I actually checked that before making the request. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What was your discovery?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is a courtroom available, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Having regard -- well, I will have to let Mr. Milovancevic respond to your submissions here. So Mr. Milovancevic, could the Trial Chamber hear from you in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this case, we have been dealing with the period covering five years, and large areas of the former Yugoslavia, the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, the operation of the United Nations and the operation of internal factors, military, political and police. The number of participants is large. The numbers of victims are large. The last witness, I will give you a general remark with reference to the specific witness, this particular witness was used by the OTP to tender large numbers of documents, large amounts of documents, by simply putting documents to witnesses -- to the witness and asking him whether he was familiar with them. The Defence had to point to the contents of some of these documents in dealing with this witness. To claim that this is a deliberate policy when the accused Martic has been sitting in the detention unit for four years, in our opinion is quite improper and something that we did not expect to hear from the Prosecutor. As far as the suggestion that the Defence should speak their mind in advance as to the length of the cross-examination is concerned, that is very well. However, I have to say right at the outset that not all the witnesses are equally significant, nor are all expert witnesses equal in terms of the weight to be accorded to their testimony. I will remind this Honourable Trial Chamber, to Mr. Grujic and Mr. Strinovic -- or, rather, Professor Strinovic, who came here as an expert, a professionist, and we had only several questions to put to him, unlike Mr. Grujic. I believe that the Trial Chamber will pass down a ruling on that matter, and I don't want to dwell on that any further. Now, as for the sitting on Friday morning, I believe that we will be able to come to an understanding. Of course, it depends on whether there is a courtroom available. However, every extra session of work requires our preparation in advance. We have been working here for several months very -- under very hard circumstances, and we believe that any additional sitting would prove to be quite taxing for the Defence, also for the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber, and, of course, last but not least for the witness himself. I am quite opposed to the suggestion that the proceedings, as lengthy as they are already, be further extended. I believe that our working week is quite taxing on us and -- as it is, and I believe that we should be quite refreshed and relaxed when coming to appear in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please don't take your seat as yet. I am very grateful for your concern for the Trial Chamber and our comfort, but other than that concern, do you have any concerns in respect of any potential for prejudice or unfairness to your client? Because that's what I would be more interested in. That's what the Trial Chamber would be more interested in, in the circumstances of the submissions made by Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for raising this issue. I believed it unnecessary to touch upon that but, of course, the health of Mr. Martic continues as it was in the past days. Every day he spends in the courtroom means that at the end of the day he has to spend at least a half an hour in the cell here, which is quite cold and uncomfortable. On several occasions, it so happened that he had to spend even more time in this cell when we were having frequent adjournments or discussing some matters. This is also something that has to be borne in mind. Of course, in addition to this, Mr. Martic has to prepare himself for every day in the courtroom and provide instructions to us. Such a course of proceeding would constitute a realistic problem for him as well. And we are grateful to the Trial Chamber for appreciating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. We crave your indulgence for a consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to learned counsel for the OTP and learned counsel for the Defence for their respective submissions. The Trial Chamber will defer the matter of a ruling until sometime tomorrow. I would like to say further that notwithstanding the submission made by learned counsel Mr. Whiting, I had intended to give a caution in a more even-handed manner to both counsel for the OTP and counsel for the Defence to try to remember the guidelines, because I think there is a duty on both sides. So before going into the evidence and calling the witness, I would ask that the OTP equally and the Defence be reminded of the business of this Court, the rules of fairness and expeditious trial, and that both sides take steps to ensure that they stay within the guidelines and that there are no infractions. So having said that, I believe we could safely call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Charles Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we are going to ask you to take your declaration now, please, before the giving of your evidence. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You may sit. Please feel very relaxed and at ease.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I start, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Richterova, please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja. Before we start, I have to apologise that we kept you waiting for such a long time. Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: My name is Charles Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, before I deal with the background information, just one procedural matter. We both speak the same language, and we should both keep in mind to keep pause between a question and answer. I'm pretty sure we will forget but we should try our best. I'm now going to go through some background information and quickly lead you through. You were born on 20th of April, 1946. You received your bachelor degree from the University of Nairobi in Kenya; you received masters degree in business administration from the York University in Toronto, Canada; and doctorate from the University of Western Ontario in Canada. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You started working for the United Nations in 1997. You held various positions related to development, economics and internal UN budgetary and management matters, and finally you were also involved in peacekeeping operations. In 1988, you were assigned to the UN Humanitarian Assistance Mission in Afghanistan as the chief of finance and administration. Between April 1992 and June 1995, you were assigned with the UN mission in the former Yugoslavia. And finally, as of 2005, you have been posted in the UN mission in Darfur as the head of the office. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus on your time in the former Yugoslavia. Can you just briefly tell us different locations you were stationed at -- during the time you were in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I arrived in the former Yugoslavia in April of 1992, in Belgrade. I was there for a couple of days, mainly to familiarise with the head of the mission, and I was asked to proceed from Belgrade through what was then known as Sector East, to Osijek in Zagreb, and then from there I went to Sector West, and then from there, I was asked to proceed to Topusko which was the headquarters of what was then known as Sector North. From there, I was there for about two years. I was also temporarily asked to take up a different assignment at the headquarters in Zagreb of the civilian Chief of Staff. After about ten months or so, I was posted to the head -- to Belgrade, where I headed that office until June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you mentioned that you spent about two years in the Sector North. The Sector North, was it then one of four designated areas so designated by the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. They were all known as UNPA, which stands for United Nations Protected Areas, and it was one of the four of those United Nations Protected Areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter Exhibit 929.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's a map, and the format is A-3 so if -- I would distribute the hard copy to assist Your Honours and Defence counsel, and, of course, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Is it on e-court at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is also on e-court but it will be very small on the e-court, so it would be easier to place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This map is taken from the concise map which is already in the exhibit. However, it was marked by the witness and also signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you -- can you tell the Judges what you highlighted on this map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. On this map, I traced approximately what was the boundaries of what I described earlier as the United Nations protected area also known as Sector North. The tracing shows two things, or three things, that I might want to draw Your Honours to. On this map, you will see -- I'm going to start here, going to the counter-clockwise. This tracing of what was approximately the border of the sector is also a representative of what you might call the line of conflict after the parties laid down their arms and it became the border between the sector on this side, which was predominantly occupied by Serbs, and the other part which represented the rest of Croatia, and this is different from this part of the border, which I'm tracing now, which represented a true boundary as it existed between the six republics that formed the former Yugoslavia. In other words, this is a boundary as it was. It also -- I wanted to highlight two points. It was an internationally recognised border, but between approximately from here, you can see Bosanska Dubica, and all the way somewhere up to here, this part of the border was nominally a border because the responsible people on both sides of the border were Serbs, and they crossed this border easily and without any hindrance from each other. On this part of the border, it represented a different reality because the people in this part of this part of the map that I'm tracing were the Muslims who lived in this area we nominally got to calling the Bihac pocket. The Serbs called Cazinska Krajina and we simply called it the Bihac pocket. This was a hard border in that sense because, on this side, there were Muslims and on this side there were the Serbs. The little X on this map also shows where our headquarters was. This is what I roughly wanted to highlight on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. It was a very exhaustive answer. I just for the record, when you said, first, that it was an internationally recognised border, between which countries? On one side it was, and on the other side it was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: On this side of this border, all of this side was what was then Bosnia and Herzegovina, as one of the six republics of the former Yugoslavia. The rest of this inside this, all of this, was what was then Croatia, and it is Croatia today's day [sic]. But this line of confrontation separated this part from the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And another thing which I would like to clarify just for the record is that certain part of the border, or on both sides of certain part of this border lived Serbs, and you started from Bosanska Dubica. Can you tell until where you indicated was this border open to both Serb sides?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. You come up to Dvor, Dvor Na Uni. That is the border of the opstina known as Dvor. And the border of Dvor would come all the way and get to -- come closer to the border of Velika Kladusa. That's where the porosity of the border stops. And I can't pinpoint here exactly where that point is. It has to be somewhere here. I can't really show it on this map exactly where that is, but conceptually the border of Dvor opstina would go all the way to the border of Velika Kladusa opstina and there is where the porosity of the border stopped. It became a hard border because the Muslims controlled the opstina of Velika Kladusa and Bihac and Cazinska. And those -- it's a long time. All these names I could be wrong about a few facts about what I have said on those -- which opstina is contiguous to what.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. You were very clear on this. And you already indicated that the cross is the location of the headquarters in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the name of that town was Topusko?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was your title when you were in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: When we went in there, it simply developed from simply civil -- chief, civil affairs coordinator, to simply -- it was later simplified to civil affairs coordinator, CAC. So some of the document will show CAC, which was for the most of the time when the title stabilised. Earlier, you might have seen some document saying CCA at the very beginning between April and May which stood or chief, civil affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. We will see this in documents which I mean to show you. But go back to the Sector North. What was your primary responsibility in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The sector, each of the four sectors, the responsibility for conducting the UN business in that sector was evenly split between the sector commander, who was a military officer, and the civilian head of that sector, which was my responsibility. The business of the UN in that sector was summarised by a document we referred to as the Vance Plan, and that is referenced often in some of the documents that you have. That document summarised our business in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So was your primary responsibility the implementation of this Vance Plan in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have heard about the Vance Plan, but can you please remind us briefly the paramount features of the Vance Plan? The main components of this Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Vance Plan was the agreement the late Cyrus Vance had concluded with the parties in the former Yugoslavia at a certain point before we arrived there outlining what it is that they -- I mean, the Serbs, the Croats -- the Serbs and the Croats were in conflict in that area, what it is they had agreed. The Vance Plan, as I say, was concluded some months before the Security Council resolution that put it into effect, allowed us to come in, and when we arrived -- I will simplify what basically the plan requested us to do. The plan, in the first and foremost intention, was to allow the parties to demobilise and lay down their arms, put their weapons in storage under United Nations custody, what was known as double-key custody, the process of demobilising and bringing these combatants to neutral. The concept was there was a recognition that there would be a political problem that led to the fighting in the first place, but the mission itself was designed so that the responsibility for finding a lasting solution was placed elsewhere, outside the mission, and that mission was specific, UNPROFOR, and different from missions before and missions after, in that it was headed by a military officer. The head of the mission was the force commander, Mr. Nambiar. The reason that I emphasise this is because there was a recognition of the political problem that was there would not be solved in the mission. It was left under something parallel to the mission that was known as the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. That was conducted and run from Geneva. Therefore, our job was, you get these combatants and these people in conflict to lay down their arms, first and foremost. Secondly, Vance Plan outlined the areas that were supposed to be in conflict and named them as opstinas in an annex. Those opstinas which in Sector North were in this area, there was the opstina of Slunj and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm really sorry to interrupt you. Maybe it would be helpful, because we in fact have this Vance Plan, and when you start talking about opstinas, maybe you would like to consult the Vance Plan. It is -- it is 65 ter number 917, and it has been exhibited under 115, if we can display it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Exhibit 115?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, it was court Exhibit 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from here, if we can go to page 5, the ERN number, yes, and down we can see Krajina on the right, there are names of the opstinas. We could highlight it. So I'm sorry to -- that I interrupted you. So you were talking about opstinas which were named in the Vance Plan, and what Vance Plan meant with these opstinas.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you are helpful. I don't think you interrupted me. You helped me rather than me named these from my head. As I began to say, he had named those opstinas as those which would comprise the area the UN was supposed to go into. As you will see, in Krajina, you see there is Kostajnica, Petrinja, Dvor, Glina, Vrginmost --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now if we could go to page 6, there is a continuation.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: You see Vojnic, you see Slunj, and Titova Korenica. I'll stop there and, if you don't mind, show you that our sector stopped just below Slunj, and the split part of that, Titova Korenica and the Sector South. So the boundary I didn't mark on the map because it's a little lower on the map that you had showed on the screen. So these were the opstinas that were named in the Vance Plan. Our -- he also proceeded to outline how day-to-day life would proceed within those opstinas when they came under the UN protection. The authority recognised in the Vance Plan was in each opstina the authority of the mayor and his chief of police. Each opstina had such an authority, under chief of police. There wasn't to be an overarching government beyond each of the opstinas. And our job was secondly to work with the authorities in each opstina, one, to return normalcy, what was expected would be a normal situation, within each opstina, have a balance of police that would represent the community, both Croats and Serbs, and achieve what was expected to be a normal situation such that those people who had been forced to flee from those sectors would return voluntarily. That also was our mandate; voluntary return of those internally displaced people or, if they left the country altogether, refugees. And to go with that, we also had a humanitarian assistance responsibility, since economic life had broken down as a result of the fighting, and therefore provision of humanitarian assistance was also a responsibility for us. But before all of that could start, demobilisation and exclusion of weapons from all of that area was a primary task, and it occupied us extremely early and went on for months before we could get to the other part of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you very clearly explained the major features of this Vance Plan. I would like to ask you: When you arrived to Sector North, it was approximately in April 1992, what was the situation there? Was the plan already going on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. When we arrived, the parties were still -- there were still remnants of conflict. Indeed, there were parties in the fox-holes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you explain? What do you mean by "fox-holes"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In there -- when militaries fight, they do define necessarily by military fiat an area of exclusion from each other where they establish a line of confrontation where they stay on their side in holes dug for defensive purposes, usually with mines in front of them, to preclude the other party from surprise attacks. So when we arrived, there were people still in position. There were tanks still smouldering when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So the process, you arrived there, and the process -- you arrived there to start the process. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can you tell us what -- what was your responsibility? What did you do to implement it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The first thing is to -- as usual in UN keeping missions is to get ourselves established, get our assets in place, meaning getting our military people, our contingents, and in this UNPA, our assets were mainly battalions or contributed member states that were to take positions when the combatants were demobilised. We also had civilian police, whom you call civil police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it -- I'm sorry again to interrupt just to make clear that the -- we are talking the same thing, the civilian police, does it -- does CIVPOL stands for civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. These were a major component of the people we needed in place so that we can get on with the job, and last but not least, we needed civil affairs and other humanitarian assistant civilians to join the mission. So on arrival, the first order of our business was I spent most of the time with the sector commander on military matters, leading to getting the combatants pull out from their front lines eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before we go any further, can you tell us little bit more about the staff you had, the number of people working for you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There wasn't a very large number of civilian staff and they were slow in getting there. Understandably. You don't get civilians ahead of military or police. The area is mined, there were few places you could stay, so it took longer to get our civilian component. And when everybody was there, I had more or less a dozen of civilians, but we also -- and when I say "civilians," I'm not counting the police, who were also part of our mandate. We had plenty of police, civilian police. We had three battalions covering the sector. In the -- in the Kostajnica and Dvor area, the Danish battalion covered that area. In the Glina and Petrinja area, the Nigerian battalion covered that area. In the Slunj and the -- part of south of Slunj all the way to Plaski near Titova Korenica, we had the Polish battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Also, is it true that representatives of ICRC, ECMM and UNHCR worked in the area of Sector North or in other sectors?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. The European monitors preceded us. They were on the ground when we arrived. There were plenty of European monitors on the ground when we arrived. ICRC was in other parts, including Bosnia and Herzegovina. UNHCR wasn't there, and because of their importance, it took me a couple months going back and forth in Zagreb to get the deployment of UNHCR into our headquarters, to -- if you recall, I mentioned earlier the issue of humanitarian assistance was of primary importance, and humanitarian assistance, the conduit for that is the UNHCR, and not having their representative on my office would have been a major deficit. So it took some months for me to get the two of them located in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you had to introduce yourself, get familiar. When you arrived, who did you meet, and let's start with the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Obviously, on the first day on my arrival, I did an internal rendezvous with the military command and the civil police command. But because the task on hand was to get the combatants to demobilise, it became immediately important that I establish contact with representatives, both on the military side and on the -- what we call and refer to in the document, the Milicija, which is simply a term for -- in Serbian for civilian police of their own, the local police. And in a military police situation like this, the first order of business is to look for a liaison to the command, and there were -- there was a structured command. So the first meeting we had was with the liaisons as well as late, immediately within a week, with the commanders of this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you -- let's start with this liaison. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. The first person -- actually, I didn't even have to look for him, he kind of looked for me, because he seemed to be kind of anxious to introduce himself and his service. His name was Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did he introduce you to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know within how short a period but it's fairly short period, maybe within a week or two, he had introduced me to first to whom he said was the commissioner of police, who was based in Vojnic, and he introduced his name, not the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you remember the name he introduced you -- or I'm sorry, I didn't phrase it correctly. What was the name he said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He told me that if I wanted anything that had to do with the police, I should contact one Toso Paic, spelled P-a-i-c, not the usual Serbian P-a-j-i-c. This was simply Paic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned -- we will go on with this a little bit later. You also mentioned that you met a commander. Who do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This one I'll preface something. The entire area that I showed you in the map, the entire sector, when we arrived, was under a military command that was actually outside the sector. It was part of the military command known as the 10th Corps. The command was in Bihac. And in the map, it's across the hard border that I described, and it is in -- it was in a place called Bihac. And the commander was a lieutenant general called Nikovic, and we had to start with him first, and then we then go to those areas -- because they had divided the entire sector in operational commands. That Sector North was divided into three operational commands. One of those command was known as Banija, and the commander was in Petrinja. The left side of that map was Kordun, and the commander was somewhere very near Topusko, and it has three offices somewhere, and his name was Cedo Bulat. And we had a third command, which is southern part covering Slunj and Plaski -- not Slunj, Plaski and a little bit below, and that was a command that was actually outside my sector. It was in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: And it was Lika command. And that I proceeded to identify each of these commands and -- on both sides of the border and did the same on the Croatian side and spent a harrowing several months with meetings with all of them, both sides of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kirudja, unfortunately, we reach 7.00, which means the end of the session for today. So we will continue tomorrow with the line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Please return tomorrow at 2.15 to continue your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're welcome. There is still some business to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber when the witness is gone. So please remain seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just would like to place on the record that during the interim period, I have received word from the Registry in respect of one of the matters affecting the ruling that is to be given; that is, whether possibly we could proceed by way of extra sittings, not to pre-empt any ruling whatsoever in the matter. And I have received word from the Registry that the other courtrooms would not be available, neither this courtroom, for hearing on Friday. So on Friday morning, my understanding is, and I have here the documents that show the sittings, which would show that all the courtrooms would be taken and in use on Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I apologise. I had -- this must have changed recently because I checked it -- oh, I see what's happened is -- I thought Courtroom III was available but I see it's been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's recent. So I apologise for the misinformation I provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I understood that it was given in good faith, but it appears that in the interim there was use made of it, intended use put down for it. So that is the position in relation to that. I think we are now in position -- in a position to close off the session, and this sitting will stand adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 25
